title: Location & Matching
description: Master geohash precision, S2 geometry cells, spatial indexing with quadtrees, nearest-driver matching with ETA, and batch matching optimization using the Hungarian algorithm.

segments.text: When a rider requests a trip, Uber needs to find the nearest available driver within seconds. In Manhattan during rush hour, there are thirty thousand active drivers. You can't check distance to all of them — that's too slow. Spatial indexing makes this a sub-millisecond operation by organizing drivers in geographic data structures.

Geohash encodes latitude and longitude into a string. 'dr5ru7' represents a rectangle in Manhattan. Longer strings mean smaller rectangles — higher precision. Geohash level six covers about one point two square kilometers. Two locations in the same geohash cell are nearby. But beware edge cases — two locations across a cell boundary can be closer than two in the same cell.

Google's S2 Geometry library maps the Earth onto a cube, then uses a Hilbert curve to assign cell IDs. Unlike geohash's rectangular grid, S2 cells are roughly equal-area everywhere on the globe — no distortion at the poles. Uber switched from geohash to S2 cells because the uniform coverage improved driver matching accuracy by fifteen percent in cities near the poles.

A quadtree recursively divides space into four quadrants. Dense areas like downtown get subdivided more — each leaf holds at most a set number of drivers. Sparse areas stay as large cells. This adaptive resolution means you check a few leaf nodes near the rider instead of scanning the entire city. Updates are O(log N) as drivers move between cells.

Finding the nearest driver isn't just geographic distance — it's ETA. A driver one kilometer away but stuck in traffic might take fifteen minutes. A driver two kilometers away on a highway might arrive in three minutes. Uber queries candidate drivers from nearby S2 cells, then calls a routing service to compute actual ETAs, and matches based on minimum ETA.

Three riders request trips simultaneously in the same neighborhood. There are four nearby drivers. Matching each rider to their individually closest driver might produce a worse total outcome than optimizing assignments globally. How would you solve this?
segments.thought_prompt: How do you optimally match N riders to M drivers when individual greedy matching is suboptimal?

segments.text: Batch matching collects requests over a short window — say two seconds — and solves the assignment problem globally. The Hungarian algorithm finds the optimal assignment that minimizes total ETA across all rider-driver pairs. Uber's implementation batches requests and solves a bipartite matching problem. This improved average ETA by eight percent in dense urban areas.

Drivers send location updates every four seconds. That's seven thousand five hundred updates per active driver per hour. With one million active drivers, that's nearly two billion location updates per hour. Each update must modify the spatial index — remove the driver from the old cell, insert into the new cell. This is why in-memory spatial indexes are essential.

Beyond reactive matching, Uber uses supply positioning — predicting where demand will spike and suggesting drivers reposition proactively. ML models trained on historical data predict demand thirty minutes ahead with seventy percent accuracy. Heat maps show drivers where to position for the best earnings. This reduces average pickup time by twelve percent.

Design the location and matching system for a ride-sharing service in a city with one hundred thousand concurrent drivers and twenty thousand ride requests per minute. What spatial index, matching algorithm, and update strategy would you use?
segments.thought_prompt: Design ride matching for 100K drivers and 20K requests/min. Spatial index + matching algorithm?

segments.text: Ride-sharing location and matching combines S2 geometry cells for uniform spatial partitioning, quadtrees for adaptive density, ETA-based matching instead of pure distance, batch optimization with the Hungarian algorithm, and ML-driven supply positioning. The spatial index is the foundation — it turns 'find nearest driver' from a full scan into a constant-time lookup.
